name: Teeth whitening pens
lead: Teeth whitening pens are over-the-counter applicator pens that brush a peroxide-based or other whitening gel onto the tooth surface. They are one of several at-home options, alongside strips, trays, rinses and whitening toothpastes.[1] The general Wikipedia article on tooth whitening does not mention pens specifically, so most of what is known comes from small laboratory studies.

In vitro work has examined how much hydrogen peroxide from pen and varnish products reaches the pulp chamber, how the products affect enamel, and how they act on tooth-coloured fillings.[2][3][4] Regulation of peroxide strength differs by region: in the EU retail products may contain up to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, while the US FDA endorses gels below 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide.[1]
infobox: Often peroxides; some use non-peroxide agents

paras: Pens deliver a small amount of gel directly onto teeth without a tray. They sit among home options that Wikipedia lists as strips, gels, rinses, toothpastes and tray systems, with in-office treatment using higher concentrations.[1] Studies group them with bleaching varnishes, which are also applied by brush.[3]

No clinical trial of whitening pens in people was identified among the sources used here; published research on pens is in vitro. A 2024 study of low-concentration bleaching varnishes, including a pen product, measured peroxide penetration into the pulp chamber and colour change in extracted premolars.[3] A 2025 Journal of Dentistry study examined pens' effect on peroxide permeability in the pulp chamber, colour and surface morphology.[5] A 2023 study tested a whitening pen on tea-stained resin composite.[6]

Broader studies of over-the-counter products have evaluated enamel microhardness, surface roughness, colour and bond strength in vitro, and a 2023 study assessed colour change, perceived aesthetics, satisfaction and side effects of such products.[2][7] A 2018 study compared two trayless at-home bleaching systems by degree of discolouration.[8] Findings are not summarised here beyond what these titles state.

Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects of peroxide whitening; Wikipedia notes sensitivity is lower with home than in-office bleaching, and that peroxide at 10 percent or higher can burn soft tissue.[1] Carbamide peroxide may roughen enamel and alter the colour of composite fillings.[1] Pulp-chamber penetration studies exist because peroxide reaching the pulp is a concern.[3][5]
Whitening is discussed as one of the cheapest ways to improve a smile, and pens are one convenient format. Wikipedia describes "bleachorexia" as an obsession with whitening.[1]

card.summary: Brush-on gel pens for at-home whitening; evidence on pens specifically is lab-only.
card.note: Peroxide limits differ by region; sensitivity and gum irritation reported with peroxide whiteners.

quick.overview:
Whitening pens are brush-on gel applicators for at-home tooth whitening, a convenient alternative to strips or trays.

Research specific to pens consists of in vitro studies of peroxide penetration, enamel effects and filling colour; no human trials of pens were found.
quick.mechanism: The gel, often peroxide-based, breaks down stain molecules on and in enamel when applied to the tooth surface.
quick.risks: Peroxide products can cause tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, and may affect enamel texture and tooth-coloured fillings. Allowed peroxide strengths differ between the EU and US.
